assertions.claim: Reid attributes the project to William H. Moore and describes publisher-procured books, documents and personal statements, including visits to officers and soldiers; he says he compared or modified material.
assertions.limit: Authorial self-description is not independent proof of the process or correctness. No particular interview, collector or original statement is tied to the 46th Ohio passage.

citations.quote: The work owes its origin to Mr. William H. Moore, the senior partner of the house by which it is published. As early as in the summer of 1863 he visited me in Washington to arrange for its preparation. Its main features were then agreed upon, and he straightway set about procuring such facts for it as were then accessible.

It was a part of the contract made by Mr. Moore on behalf of the publishers, that they should procure for me all books, documentary matter, personal statements, etc., necessary for the preparation of the work. In pursuance of this arrangement, they have employed persons of apparent fitness for such service to visit the armies in the field, and, since the close of the war to wait upon officers of regiments, Generals, private soldiers—upon any one, in short, who might be thought able to contribute any fact not yet known or cast light upon any occurrence hitherto ill-understood.

With the material thus furnished my own work began. Many of the statements I was able to correct or modify from personal knowledge—many more could be verified from published documents or from official reports on file at the War Department—still others could be compared with the versions given in the reports of battles and of investigating committees, and in other documentary matter published by the Rebel Congress, of which I was fortunate enough to procure nearly complete sets at Richmond.

assertions.claim: The preface, dated December 24, 1867, credits Major Frank E. Miller with organizing supplied material and preparing indexes.
assertions.limit: General assistance does not identify Miller as the author, informant or eyewitness behind volume II p.286. The prefatory date is not the narrative or interview date.

citations.quote: I am specially indebted to Major Frank E. Miller (of Washington C. H., Ohio) for intelligent and valuable assistance in reducing to shape the vast mass of material placed in my hands by the publishers. He has also prepared the exhaustive indexes which accompany the work.

assertions.claim: The inspected 46th Ohio narrative on volume II pp.286–289 supplies no named contributor or source footnote for the overnight passage.
assertions.limit: A bounded negative across these four narrative pages and preface pp.1–2, not proof that Reid had no source or that no attribution exists elsewhere. Officers mentioned as actors are not automatically informants.

citations.quote: The regiment was posted a short distance to the right of Shiloh Church, and there it remained in comparative quiet until the battle. On Saturday, April 5th, companies B and K were on picket. During the night the enemy was feeling the lines constantly, and at daylight his columns could be seen deploying in the distance. At sunrise a Rebel cavalry officer emerged from the woods within thirty yards of the picket-line, and, checking his horse, he stood for a moment in seeming composure, and then inquired: "Are these Union pickets?" He was told they were, and was ordered to come up.

assertions.claim: Lindsey p.18 repeats the B/K picket and constant overnight feeling language and much of the sunrise encounter, with small wording differences from Reid.
assertions.limit: Inference: this is a possible textual transmission or common-source link, not established independent corroboration or proved direct copying. The original witness, post identity and continuous firing remain unknown. Copyright 1903 does not date its underlying evidence.
